profile.reading:
CloudHQ MCC3 sits at 10740 Airman Avenue, Manassas, Virginia, part of CloudHQ's MCC Campus, which the company's own current campus page describes as "CloudHQ's original campus location," on the south side of Manassas in Prince William County, connected to CloudHQ's adjacent "MDC campus" and to regional fiber via the "Manassas Fiber Highway." CloudHQ states the full MCC Campus totals 2,232,875 square feet and 382 megawatts of total critical IT load across seven data centers, with 96 megawatts currently available; the company's current site describes MCC5 as site-plan approved and ready for immediate development and MCC7's construction as beginning mid-2025 with an expected Q3 2026 ready-for-service date, but does not individually disclose MCC3's present-day capacity, so the campus total is not applied to this specific building, and no third-party aggregator figure specific to MCC3 was found either. CloudHQ was founded in 2016 by Hossein Fateh, who also founded QTS Realty Trust and, per CloudHQ's own materials, was the first person in the United States to obtain an IRS ruling allowing data center income to qualify for real estate investment trust tax treatment. CloudHQ is privately held through the Fateh Family Office, with regional headquarters in Washington DC, London, and Singapore, and states a company-wide net-zero emissions target by 2040. CloudHQ does not name a power utility for the MCC Campus on its current site.

Prince William County's Manassas-area data center corridor has grown alongside Loudoun County's much larger Ashburn cluster, though the two submarkets have followed somewhat different zoning and community-engagement trajectories; Prince William County has seen significant public debate in recent years over large-scale data center rezoning proposals near residential areas and historic sites, though this profile does not confirm CloudHQ's MCC Campus specifically as a party to any particular zoning controversy without independent sourcing. CloudHQ's global portfolio spans 23 campuses and more than 30 million square feet across six countries, with more than 1,380 megawatts of critical IT load already contracted company-wide.

reading.body:
CloudHQ MCC3 publishes 2.2 million square feet of technical space but no megawatt figure, making its actual power capacity and compute density unknowable from operator disclosures.

The operator's facility page lists footprint alone. No critical IT load in megawatts, no power specification, and no uptime tier appear in published specifications. This omission is common enough that Virginia's twenty largest data center facilities by disclosed megawatts represent only 1,326 MW across nineteen sites, while hundreds of smaller or non-disclosing facilities exist across the state. Without a power figure, facility size becomes mere real estate information. Two million square feet could house dense, power-constrained equipment or sparse, redundant infrastructure. That uncertainty collapses when a megawatt number lands.

CloudHQ operates this campus as part of a seven-building cluster totaling 382 MW of critical IT load with 96 MW available. The company itself manages more than 1,380 MW of contracted capacity globally and describes more than 6,000 MW of expansion potential. The gap between what an operator publishes for a single facility and what it reports for itself at scale suggests this campus is material to CloudHQ's footprint. What remains opaque is whether MCC3 itself constrains by power, by real estate, or by something else. Manassas sits in a different power district than Loudoun County's cluster to its east. That distinction matters if grid capacity, not building square footage, is what shapes where compute can actually scale next.
